narrative:
The model estimated a 66.3% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is a risk estimate, not a certainty, but it was high enough that your application was denied under the school’s process.

The strongest factor by far was your third-year class standing. A third-year decile of 1, compared with an average of about 5.8 among accepted students, strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Your first-year standing was less important: a decile of 5 was below the accepted-student average of 6, yet in this assessment it modestly pushed toward passing. It was not enough to offset the third-year signal. Your LSAT score of 34, below the accepted average of 37.18, was the smallest of the three influences and, in this particular combination, slightly pushed toward passing rather than failure. The ranking matters: third-year standing dominated, while the other two were secondary.

To strengthen a future application, focus on areas you can change. Consider retaking the LSAT only if practice tests show a meaningful gain, and take additional coursework or a structured program that demonstrates readiness for advanced legal study. Seek admissions and bar-preparation counseling, and prepare a brief, factual explanation of your third-year performance and any circumstances behind it. Apply to programs that use holistic review and can weigh your trend, preparation plan, and personal context alongside the numbers.
